overview: Player ESP is a wall-hack renderer with a single registered event handler. On every Render3DEvent it walks mc.theWorld.loadedEntityList and, for each EntityPlayer other than the local player, calls RenderUtils.drawEsp(o, new Color(0, 0, 0, 21).getRGB()), which draws a 1x2 block axis-aligned box around the entity position (posX plus or minus 0.5, posY to posY + 2.0). The color is hardcoded near-transparent black: the module exposes no settings at all, no color picker, no box mode, no tracer option. It is wire-silent: the handler only reads the client-side entity mirror and issues GL11 calls, so no packet leaves the client and no server-side check can observe it.

sections.p: The module is one Consumer<Render3DEvent> registered with the client event bus. Each fired event loops the loaded entity list, skips the local player and anything that is not an EntityPlayer, and renders the survivors with a fixed translucent color. drawEsp forwards to RenderUtils.box with the color object, and the surrounding enableGL2D and disableGL2D helpers configure GL11 blending (source 770, destination 771), line smoothing and depth state for the frame. There are no settings: the constructor registers only the keybind 0 and the render category.

The rendered state is the client's mirror of server broadcasts. S0C spawn-player packets create the EntityPlayer entries with position and rotation, and the entity-move and teleport packets (S14 family, S18) keep those entries current; the module draws each frame from that live state, so a player's current position is outlined regardless of occlusion. S0F spawn-mob packets populate non-player entries that the instanceof EntityPlayer filter discards, so the renderer is players-only by construction. The 1x2 box spans the standing entity bounds, posX plus or minus 0.5 to posY + 2.0.

The module produces no network traffic of its own and changes no server-visible state. It cannot be inferred from the outside because the GL11 calls never leave the client, and the entity list it reads is data every vanilla client also receives and renders. The honest conclusion is that no server-side anticheat mechanism can detect this module; the countering entries below therefore describe the checks that police the data stream it consumes and the aim behavior it typically enables, each with the boundary stated explicitly.

files.label: ESP.java (module)
files.explanation: The module is the onEvent field, a Consumer<Render3DEvent> that walks mc.theWorld.loadedEntityList, filters to EntityPlayer instances other than the local player, and renders each with RenderUtils.drawEsp(o, new Color(0, 0, 0, 21).getRGB()). The fixed color and the absence of any settings are the defining traits: the constructor takes only the display name, keybind 0 and the RENDER category, so there is no configurable surface at all.

files.label: RenderUtils.java (drawEsp renderer)
files.explanation: RenderUtils provides the drawEsp overloads and the GL11 state helpers the module relies on. drawEsp(Entity) calls box(o.posX - 0.5, o.posY, o.posZ - 0.5, o.posX + 0.5, o.posY + 2.0, o.posZ + 0.5, new Color(c2)), a 1x2 block axis-aligned box at the entity's current position, and the enableGL2D and disableGL2D helpers wrap the frame with blend, depth-mask and line-smoothing state. The whole module effect is one call into this class, which is why the file is the natural companion for the full-source page.

countering.label: Grim PacketEntityReplication (entity state handler)
countering.explanation: PacketEntityReplication is Grim's consumer for the spawn and entity-update broadcasts, maintaining the server-side mirror of entity state that the prediction engine reads. The module renders the client-side mirror of exactly the same stream, so this handler is the closest server-side counterpart to what ESP draws, and the honest finding is a gap: the handler validates and tracks entity data, but client rendering is invisible to it, so the module cannot be detected through this path. The check matters here as the description of the data ESP consumes, not as a detection mechanism.

countering.label: NCP fight Angle (wall-aim rotation stream)
countering.explanation: The realistic detection surface for an ESP user is the aim behavior it enables: a player who knows enemy positions through walls aims at wall-hidden targets, producing a rotation stream with no visible target and target switches without yaw motion. NCP fight Angle scores exactly those signals inside a 1000ms window with 0.98 decay, but it is config-gated and dormant at the stock thresholds in this tree (move 100, time 150, yaw 60, switch 50). ESP alone emits no rotation at all, so the check is an honest boundary: it polices the companion aim, never the renderer.

countering.label: Hawk EntityInteractDirection (server ray validation)
countering.explanation: EntityInteractDirection ray traces from the server-observed yaw and pitch to the victim with a 0.2 box expansion and fails any C02 attack whose facing cone misses the target. An ESP-informed aura that attacks a wall-hidden player fails this check the moment the victim is off the facing cone, because the server's ray passes through the wall while the client aimed at the ESP outline. The boundary is explicit: the module itself sends no C02, so the check only ever sees the pairing, and a pure ESP user who never attacks is invisible to it.

countering.label: Hawk AimbotConvergence (fixed-point lock)
countering.explanation: AimbotConvergence tracks whether a player's ray converges on a fixed point across consecutive moves, with convergence scored when the squared distance to the lock point falls below 1e-8; a smooth aim that repeatedly returns to the same point across ticks is the signature. An ESP-assisted aimbot locks onto the outline's center, which is a fixed point the server's own geometry never corroborates, so the convergence signature builds. As with the other boundary checks, ESP alone produces no rotation stream, so the check fires only on the companion aim module.
